blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: streets and boundaries

items.t: The FVRD describes Electoral Area E as "in the North Cascade mountains" and known as the Chilliwack River Valley, with a population of 1,568 (2021 Census) across 652 square kilometres.
Chilliwack Lake Road is the valley's only spine: addresses in the valley are on Chilliwack Lake Road, for example Thompson Regional Park at 48600 Chilliwack Lake Road.

The named communities in the valley, from the FVRD's slope assessment, are Baker Trails, Bell Acres, Slesse Park and Post Creek, spread along the slopes on both sides of the river from Baker Trails in the east to the Slesse Park landslide in the west.
No official document publishes street-by-street boundaries for the "Chilliwack River Valley" as a neighbourhood; the Electoral Area E boundary is the governing line.

blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: the housing stock

items.t: The valley's stock is rural and detached: the FVRD's Housing Needs Report for Electoral Areas E and H reports most housing units are single detached (78%) and movable dwellings make up 21% of dwelling units, figures that cover Electoral Areas E and H combined, not the valley alone.

The same report records that the only permitted residential use under the Official Community Plan's designations for these areas is single-family, so there is no strata or multi-family product planned into the valley's plan frame.

blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: rules that affect buyers

items.t: 1115, 2011, was adopted by the FVRD Board on August 13, 2013, and Amendment Bylaw No. 1533, 2019 renamed the plan for Electoral Areas E and H after the former Area E was split in 2014.

River erosion has its own legal line here: an OCP amendment adopted in 2021 implemented an Erosion Setback Line in the Wilson Road to Baker Trails area and the Slesse Park area, based on two reports on the Chilliwack River.

The FVRD judges new building in hazard areas against its Hazard Acceptability Thresholds for Development Approvals, which include a specific table for Chilliwack River Valley erosion or avulsion measured against the erosion setback line and the 100-year erosion limit line.
Where the erosion or avulsion threat is immediate and extreme, the thresholds state a building permit may not be available until approved bank protection is provided.

blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: Thompson Regional Park at 48600 Chilliwack Lake Road is the valley's community park: a 3-hectare FVRD park donated by the Chilliwack River Valley Ratepayers Association, with a covered picnic shelter, a playground, an easy 1-kilometre loop trail along a salmon enhancement channel, flush toilets and parking, open 7 a.m. to sunset.

The valley's upper end is a provincial park, not a townsite: Sx̱ótsaqel/Chilliwack Lake Provincial Park has 182 frontcountry campsites, 40 kilometres of trails and backcountry camps at Greendrop, Lindeman, Flora and Radium Lakes, and its gates are locked between 11 p.m. and 7 a.m. daily.
Chilliwack Lake has severe afternoon winds and dangerous currents at its outflow, on BC Parks' safety information — a fact that matters for any property pitched on lake or river recreation.

Chilliwack River Provincial Park, on the river along Chilliwack Lake Road, was established in 1961 and has floodplain characteristics, and BC Parks states the river supports steelhead and chum, coho and sockeye salmon.

The FVRD's own service list for Area E is short and specific: Area E Community Parks, Fire Protection, Dyke Operations and Maintenance, Storm Drainage, Street Lighting, Transit and Water — a buyer should check which of these a specific property actually receives.
There is no library branch and no recreation centre in the valley: the nearest Fraser Valley Regional Library branch is Sardis Library at 5819 Tyson Road in Chilliwack.

SD33's Long Range Facilities Plan notes the district does not bus students from south to north or vice versa given the geography of some schools, especially at the periphery of the district — the valley is exactly that periphery case.

The valley's history runs through it: BC Parks records that the Hudson's Bay Company cut the first recorded trail up the Chilliwack River in 1855, improving the Indigenous trail that joined the nine Indigenous villages between Vedder Crossing and Chilliwack Lake.

blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: development and new projects

items.t: Chilliwack River Valley Slope Stability Risk Assessment — Fraser Valley Regional District with BGC Engineering, fully funded by the BC Ministry of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness: a technical assessment, mapping and modelling project for slope hazards from Baker Trails in the east to the Slesse Park landslide in the west, plus the Ranger Run area and the Post Creek subdivision, intended to assess the safety of existing lands, infrastructure, development and residents and to identify mitigation options, including under future climate conditions. Status: assessment underway, with a community survey that received 108 responses and a community workshop planned in the valley this winter; page last updated December 6, 2025 (as of November 3, 2026).

Wilson Road Dike flood recovery repairs — Fraser Valley Regional District: flood recovery repairs along the Wilson Road Dike, with pedestrian access restricted during the work. Status: repairs scheduled August 17 to September 25, 2026 (as of November 3, 2026).

blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: costs and taxes

items.t: The FVRD's 2026 Electoral Area E residential utility rates are narrow and named: Water — Bell Acres, billed quarterly, metered, minimum $86.00 with usage over 50 cubic metres at $1.77 per cubic metre, and Baker Trails Sewer, a flat $1,021.78 billed annually.

FVRD utility bills are issued every three months in January, April, July and October, as user fees in addition to taxation, and the FVRD notes not all taxpayers in the same electoral area are included in the same service.

blocks.text: Chilliwack River Valley: risks and due diligence

items.t: Slope hazards are the headline risk and they are named individually: the FVRD assessment covers landslides, debris flows, rotational slumps, rockfall and rockslides, and it expressly focuses on geohazards rather than flooding or wildfire, so a buyer needs separate checks for those.

River erosion is a permit-level constraint, not background information: the FVRD's hazard thresholds score new building, subdivision and rezoning against the erosion setback line and the 100-year erosion limit line for the Chilliwack River Valley, and a covenant acknowledging future erosion hazard is implied in approvals in the middle band.

Wildfire and evacuation planning are FVRD documents a buyer can read before offering: the Area E page links a Community Wildfire Resiliency Plan, an Emergency Management Plan, an Evacuation Guide for Area E and a Hazard Report, and the FVRD runs emergency notifications through Alertable.

Dike protection here is an FVRD service, not a city one: Dyke Operations and Maintenance is listed among Area E's local services, and the Wilson Road Dike needed flood recovery repairs in 2026 — ask which dike, if any, protects the specific property.

blocks.text: More from Jared on River Valley
River Valley appeals to fishing and recreation buyers, acreage buyers priced out of Chilliwack and Sardis, and full-time residents who commute into the city.

faq.a: No School District 33 (SD33) public school is located in the valley: the BC Ministry of Education's list of SD33 schools shows no school with a Chilliwack Lake Road or valley address, with district schools instead in Chilliwack, Sardis, Cultus Lake, Yarrow, Greendale and Rosedale.
faq.q: Which schools serve a Chilliwack Lake Road address?

faq.a: No fixed-route bus runs into the valley: BC Transit's Chilliwack and FVRD Transit Future Action Plan states the Chilliwack Conventional Transit System provides fixed-route, fixed-schedule service within the City of Chilliwack, and none of its nine listed routes enters the Chilliwack River Valley. The one exception is accessible transit — BC Transit's Chilliwack Rider's Guide states residents of Chilliwack River Valley and Cultus Lake North may be eligible for handyDART, its door-to-door service for people who cannot use fixed-route transit without assistance.
faq.q: Is there bus service in the valley?

faq.a: That dead zone is a practical fact for showings, inspections and emergency calls for properties toward the lake end of the road, and it is one reason the FVRD pushes residents to sign up for Alertable emergency notifications.
faq.q: Will my phone work at the property?

faq.a: It depends on which named settlement the property is in, and most addresses are on neither FVRD system: the FVRD's 2026 Electoral Area E rates list one water service area, Bell Acres (metered), and one sewer service area, Baker Trails (flat annual charge).
